extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, journalists, and researchers interested in media, propaganda, and journalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for recognizing and characterizing 'news propaganda'—propaganda covertly packaged as credible news—including its transparency, accuracy, motives, effects, and typical dissemination media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of source and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: News propaganda is covertly packaged as credible news but without sufficient transparency concerning the news item's source and the motivation behind its release. "Transparency of the source is one parameter critical to distinguish between news propaganda and traditional news press releases and video news releases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of clear sourcing or undisclosed sponsors/motivations is a key indicator that a piece is propaganda rather than straightforward news. Compare item metadata, bylines, disclosures, and whether the originator's interests are made explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (Black/Gray/White propaganda distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accuracy of this type of information, or lack thereof, puts the propaganda into the Black Propaganda or Gray Propaganda categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual accuracy and verifiability. Systematic falsehoods or fabricated elements point toward 'black' propaganda; mixed-accuracy or misleading context may be 'gray'. Accuracy helps classify the severity and type of propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declared or undeclared purpose/motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: News propaganda may be spread for widely different reasons including governance, political or ideological motivations, partisan agendas, religious or ethnic reasons, and commercial or business motivations; their purposes are not always clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the likely beneficiaries and intended audience. If the content advances a clear partisan, commercial, ideological, or state agenda—especially without disclosure—that suggests propaganda. Consider whether messaging aligns with known strategic objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on ideals: supporting vs eroding
rubrics_metrics.description: Jason Stanley defines the characteristics of propaganda as the service of either supporting or eroding ideals. The first distinction between kinds of propaganda has to do with whether or not it erodes or supports the ideals it appears to embody. This is the distinction between supporting and undermining propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the piece reinforces the stated values/ideals (supporting propaganda) or undermines them while appearing to uphold them (undermining). Consider rhetorical strategies and implicit value signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging/presentation as credible news
rubrics_metrics.description: News propaganda is 'propaganda packaged as credible news' — presented in news formats and genres so as to appear legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for use of journalistic conventions (headlines, bylines, datelines, report-like structure, quotes, 'exclusive' framing) used to lend credibility despite lacking standard editorial transparency or fact-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and format vulnerability (print, broadcast, new media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media vary in how commonly and easily they have been used to disseminate news propaganda: historically print has been less common; radio and television have been prominent (e.g., WWII radio, television's 24-hour cycle); new media and social media have made spread more accessible and scalable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the medium when assessing risk: broadcast and social platforms can amplify messaging rapidly and may bypass editorial gatekeeping. New media also enables state and non-state actors to deploy information warfare tactics (e.g., coordinated posts, viral amplification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and timing (e.g., war, domestic upheaval, national security)
rubrics_metrics.description: News propaganda can be motivated by national security reasons, especially in times of war or domestic upheaval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the historical and situational context: spikes in propaganda are often correlated with conflicts, crises, or politically sensitive moments. Timing relative to events can signal strategic intent.
